transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-11-22
- Time: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 42 minutes
- Attendees: Ethan Morales, Priya Shah (Redwood); Nora Blake, Samir Patel, Renee Gomez (Archipelago)

Summary:
Archipelago AI is evaluating Redwood for a customer-facing streaming chat product that regularly experiences sudden token surges (batch invites, notifications). They need guidance on hosted vs dedicated vs private, concrete p95 latency targets for first byte and streaming throughput (tokens/sec), and an initial benchmark plan to validate concurrency and warmup behavior. Security (SOC 2, KMS, audit logs) and EU data residency are requirements.

Topics: p95 targets, concurrency, streaming tokens/sec, prefix/KV caching, batching, Dedicated cluster sizing, private deployment considerations, SOC2/KMS, cost tradeoffs.

Action items (recap in call): see metadata list above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Ethan: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Ethan from Redwood, i'm joined by Priya on the se side, how are you all?
[00:12] Nora: good, thanks. we wanted to focus on throughput for the surge scenario and streaming latencies. we have a pretty spiky workload.
[00:20] Priya: great, can you give us the current numbers and what you mean by "surge"? rough qps, payload sizes, token lengths?
[00:29] Samir: yeah so typical session is around 80-120 tokens per turn, average user typing leads to streaming at about 25 tokens/sec. spikes happen when we push invites or when a cohort gets redirected — that can mean 1500 concurrent streaming sessions for like 5-10 minutes.
[00:45] Renee: to add infra detail, our current infra is k8s on GCP, we have autoscaling for frontends but model serving is our bottleneck. we tried a managed endpoint but costs exploded at peak.
[01:05] Ethan: OK. the two p95 metrics customers usually care about are first-byte latency (time to first token) and steady-state token latency (per-token). what's your p95 SLO target today?
[01:17] Nora: we were hoping for first-byte p95 < 400ms for short replies, and end-to-end for 120-token completions p95 < 1.2s, but not sure if that's realistic for bursty concurrency.
[01:30] Priya: that's achievable in some configs. on Hosted we can often hit ~300-500ms first byte for 1-2k rps depending on model size and batching; Dedicated gives more predictable headroom because you reserve GPU pools and tune batch sizes and cache.
[01:48] Samir: can you explain how caching helps for streaming? heard about kv cache but not sure how it interacts with token/sec.
[01:55] Priya: sure — prefix and KV caching reduce compute for previously seen prefix tokens, which helps for multi-turn state. for streaming it's more about warm KV cache and not recomputing past context. also continuous batching and batching windows let us pack short requests to increase throughput — but batching has tradeoffs with first-byte latency.
[02:20] Renee: how does Redwood handle cold starts and warmup during a surge? if 1500 sessions spin up, do we see degraded p95 for minutes?
[02:28] Ethan: good question. Dedicated can keep a warm pool with minimum residency to avoid cold starts; Hosted has warm routing heuristics and fast spin up but can be less deterministic. we also do prewarmed containers and fast model load paths — but for very large spikes, we recommend a Dedicated pool or burst buckets on Hosted.
[02:50] Speaker 4: (audio low) sorry missed that — what was the thing about burst?
[02:56] Priya: we can configure burst capacity: for Dedicated you reserve GPUs and allow autoscale to add more; for Hosted we can route to higher tier instances temporarily, but it depends on account limits.
[03:10] Samir: for benchmarking, we want a plan that measures: first-byte p95, steady-state tokens/sec per session, aggregate tokens/sec at peak, and p95 for streaming inter-token. do you have a spreadsheet or script?
[03:22] Ethan: yes, we'll send a benchmark plan that includes: sample request traces, a config matrix (model size, batch window, KV caching on/off), and streaming client scripts (curl + websocket and SDK). will also include example yaml for Dedicated cluster sizing.
[03:36] Nora: cost — how do we estimate cost for Dedicated vs Hosted at our expected usage? we care about predictable monthly costs during big events.
[03:44] Priya: Dedicated is committed resource -> predictable. you size for your concurrent sessions and expected tokens/sec. we give guidance: e.g., for a 70B model on A100-ish class, you might get X concurrent streams at Y tokens/sec. for Hosted we show historical unit costs and suggest autoscale policies with burst credit. we'll provide a cost matrix in the doc.
[04:08] Renee: security — we must be SOC2-compliant and use KMS keys. also EU data residency for some customers and audit logs for data exports.
[04:18] Ethan: Redwood supports SOC2, customer-managed KMS/HSM for Private, and audit logs for all modes. Private deployment (VPC or on-prem) gives the strongest controls. i'll attach the SOC2 and architecture docs.
[04:33] Samir: what about streaming token rates? we saw some Redwood docs saying 30-60 tokens/sec per stream; is that a hard limit?
[04:41] Priya: not a hard limit — sustained token/sec depends on model size and GPU throughput. smaller models and quantized pathways get higher tokens/sec. network and client-side also matter. in our pilots we've seen steady 80+ tokens/sec per stream on optimized stacks.
[04:58] Nora: ok, example target for us then: first-byte p95 < 400ms, per-token latency so that a 120-token generation completes in <1.2s p95, and system supports 1500 concurrent streams at 25 tokens/sec average for 10 minute spikes. any gotchas?
[05:15] Priya: main caveats: batching windows increase throughput but add latency for first token; KV cache effectiveness is workload-dependent; you should also instrument token-level tracing in your app. we'll recommend a canary with realistic traffic and include a tracing hook.
[05:32] Ethan: we'll also measure tail behavior — 99th percentile spike behavior — and profile memory/KV cache hits.
[05:40] Samir: weird question — do you do any re-routing if a region is saturated? we need cross-region fallback.
[05:46] Priya: yes, smart routing can failover to another region or model variant (smaller model) to preserve availability. you can set policies for latency vs cost.
[05:57] Renee: regarding private deployment, how heavy is the ops? our infra team wants low-touch.
[06:03] Ethan: Private requires more ops (you manage networking and infra), but Redwood Private includes a control plane that can be run in VPC; we offer an on-prem package too. Dedicated is sort of middle ground — we manage infra but you get reservation and isolation.
[06:20] Nora: timeline — if pilot goes well, we want to go into a 3-month limited rollout next quarter.
[06:26] Ethan: that sounds reasonable. we'll aim to have the benchmark plan and sizing options over the next 3 business days.
[06:33] Samir: ok last technical — how do you measure streaming p95? is it first-byte or inter-token?
[06:39] Priya: both. we define: first-byte latency = time from request to first token; inter-token latency = average per-token time during streaming; total time = end-to-end. our scripts will capture all three and produce p50/p95/p99.
[06:55] Speaker 4: quick Q — do you support SAML SSO for C-suite access?
[06:59] Ethan: yes, SAML/SSO + RBAC are supported for Console and audit logs.
[07:05] Nora: thanks, can you include example A/B fallback policies (if small model ok) in the doc?
[07:10] Priya: yes we'll include a sample routing policy that falls back to a smaller quantized model when latency crosses thresholds.
[07:18] Ethan: recap and next steps — Ethan will send benchmark plan + streaming scripts; Priya will draft Dedicated sizing and cost matrix; Renee will share traffic patterns; we’ll schedule the pilot kickoff for week of Dec 6.
[07:35] Nora: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
